English Reformation
ING-glish ref-or-MAY-shuhn
noun (church history)
From England + Reformation (Latin reformare, to form anew); the sixteenth-century breaking of the English church from Rome and its gradual reform by the Word of God.

Biblical Definition

The English Reformation is the sixteenth-century recovery of the gospel in England, begun in tangled motives and brought to fruition by faithful men and the blood of martyrs. It opened with Henry VIII's self-serving breach with Rome over his marriage — a political act, not a converted heart — yet God overruled a king's sin for the freeing of His Word. William Tyndale had already given England the Scriptures in her own tongue and was strangled and burned for it, praying that the Lord would open the king of England's eyes. Under Edward VI, Thomas Cranmer gave the church the Book of Common Prayer and the Forty-Two Articles, planting a Reformed liturgy and confession. Mary Tudor's reign drove the work back in fire: Cranmer, Latimer, and Ridley were burned at Oxford, Latimer bidding Ridley "play the man" and light such a candle as should never be put out. Under Elizabeth the settlement held, and the Thirty-Nine Articles fixed a Reformed doctrine within an episcopal frame. From this soil sprang the Puritans, who judged the Reformation half-finished and pressed for a purer church — and from the Puritans, in time, the Baptists whose confession this dictionary owns.

Webster 1828 Definition

The sixteenth-century recovery of the gospel in England — begun in Henry VIII's political breach with Rome, advanced by Tyndale's Bible and Cranmer's Prayer Book, sealed by the Oxford martyrs under Mary, and settled in the Thirty-Nine Articles. From its Puritan fruit sprang the Baptists.

ENGLISH REFORMATION, noun. The reforming of the church in England in the sixteenth century by the recovery of Scripture and the gospel.

Begun politically in Henry VIII's breach with Rome (1534), but rooted spiritually in Tyndale's English Bible.

Advanced under Edward VI by Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer and the Articles of Religion.

Sealed in fire under Mary Tudor: Cranmer, Latimer, and Ridley burned at Oxford.

Settled under Elizabeth in the Thirty-Nine Articles; its Puritan fruit bore, in time, the Baptists.

Key Scripture

Psa 119:130 — "The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple."

2 Tim 2:9 — "Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound."

John 8:32 — "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."

Rev 2:10 — "be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."

Modern Corruption

The age flattens the English Reformation into mere Tudor politics — a king's divorce dressed up as religion — and so misses the gospel God brought through it; others romanticize the medieval church it left and call the recovery a needless rupture.

expand to see more

Modern secular history tells the English Reformation as nothing but power and appetite: Henry wanted a wife and an heir, dissolved the monasteries for their gold, and religion was the pretext. There is real sin in that telling, and the dictionary does not whitewash Henry. But to stop there is to be blind to what God did: an open Bible in the plowman's tongue, a preached gospel, justification by faith recovered, and martyrs who died not for a king's marriage but for Christ. The Lord is not hindered from working His good through the crooked motives of men.

A second corruption runs the other way — the modern romanticizing of pre-Reformation England as a golden age of faith wickedly torn apart. This forgets the indulgences, the locked-up Scriptures, the gospel buried under merit and Mass. The Reformation was not a rupture of a healthy church but the recovery of a sick one. The principle to keep is that the Word of God, once loosed, cannot be bound (2 Tim 2:9); England's reform stands or falls by that Word, not by the worthiness of the kings who unwittingly served it.

Hebrew Roots

From Latin reformare (to form anew); the English branch of the wider Reformation, rooted in Tyndale's Bible, Cranmer's liturgy, and the Oxford martyrs.

expand to see more

Latin reformare, to form anew, restore to true shape

Tyndale's English New Testament (1526) — the Word in the people's tongue

Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer and the Articles of Religion

The Oxford martyrs — Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley — under Mary Tudor

The Thirty-Nine Articles (1571), settling a Reformed doctrine in England

Usage

"The English Reformation gave the plowman a Bible he could read and the martyrs a gospel worth burning for."

"Latimer's word at the stake — "we shall this day light such a candle" — is the English Reformation in a sentence."

"From the unfinished work of the English Reformation the Puritans and then the Baptists pressed on toward a purer church."
